messages.subject: Dynamic multistate occupancy advice
messages.subject_clean: Dynamic multistate occupancy advice
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am seeking advice on using a multistate dynamic occupancy
model framework. I have 39 sites in a river that were surveyed under a robust
design. Surveys on 2 consecutive days in a month form secondary periods when
occupancy state is assumed static. Sites were surveyed again after a few weeks,
and these “monthly” survey events form the primary periods between which
occupancy state changes. In years 1 and 2, there were four primary events
spanning February to June, and in year 3 there were five primary events during
these months. The target species is migratory and enters the river each year
and, we hypothesize, increases the proportion of occupied sites as more individuals
immigrate and move further upriver.

 We think that two different size groups (small and large) have
different initial occupancy and colonization rates. The states are unoccupied
(0), occupied by small and large fish (1), and conditional on occupied, occupied
only by large fish (2). These states have nothing to do with reproduction, small
fish being present is not a result of spawning but due to differential
migratory behavior.

 Environmental conditions varied across years, which could
lead to initial occupancy for states 1 and 2 to vary across years (or not). Similarly,
colonization rates may vary across years as well as by state.

Initially, I ran separate dynamic occupancy models for each size class and each year using colext function from unmarked. However, a reviewer was not satisfied with this approach and suggested that I do not separate the dataset to dataset. Hence, the multistate framework to account for different size groups. But, I am unsure how to set this up so that I can test if initial occupancy or colonization probabilities vary across years. Any suggestions are welcome, as are recommended readings. I have not been able to find an analogous example since most studies only look at primary periods within a single year or treat years as the primary periods.

Thanks in advance.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Single season single species occupancy model
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Single season single species occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Satavisha,

no, with a single site you can't separate the two parameter types in an occupancy: i.e., the probs of occupancy and detection. And more importantly, when you aggregate (that's what's meant by 'club', right ?) the original 3 sites to a single one, then it is impossible in principle to explain any variation among sites, because there is no variation among sites.

Even if you keep the original 3 sites separate, I would not recommend fitting any models with site covariates, because that would correspond to a regression with just 3 data points.

Sorry can't be more positive here.

Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

The information about the 'bup' function indicates that it stores the posterior distribution of the latent variables. I have been using this function to obtain site-level abundance of a species, analyzed with 'gdistsamp'. However, this function allows to estimate both species abundance and density with the argument "output". After running both, I found that the posterior estimates of both models were roughly the same, therefore I assume no matter what output is specified, the posterior estimates obtained with 'bup' correspond to the species abundance, right?
Thank you for your comments.
Best
Julien

messages.subject_clean: AW: [unmarked] Dynamic multistate occupancy advice
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tyler,

here are some tentative thoughts; other thoughts, including dissent, very welcome 😊

I would see the benefit of a multistate model mostly in the case where you think there is either some interaction among the small and the large class of the fish or when you’re interested in the transition rates among the states among primary periods, or in rates of state assigment errors.

However, you seem to want to compare some of the parameters among the two classes of fish, and you don’t seem to be interested in interactions, transitions or assignment errors. Thus, one simplistic analysis would simply be a dynocc model stratified by size class. Thus, you stack the two data sets on top of each other and add a factor for “large” and “small” and then test for effects of that factor on whatever parameter you’re interested.

The only snag is that this analysis would do some pseudo-replication, i.e., ignore possible dependencies in the data due to the fact that each physical site (per year, visit) occurs twice in your response data. In the simplest case, this might perhaps just make your SEs/CIs a little too small and you could obtain adequate uncertainty intervals by some sort of non-parametric bootstrapping ? Or alternatively, you might fit random site effects into every parameter. This should now work in the latest versions of unmarked owing to the power of TMB.

I am not really sure about this, but I do think that multistate modeling is overkill for your research questions.

Best regards  --- Marc

Betreff: [unmarked] Dynamic multistate occupancy advice

Hello,

I am seeking advice on using a multistate dynamic occupancy model framework. I have 39 sites in a river that were surveyed under a robust design. Surveys on 2 consecutive days in a month form secondary periods when occupancy state is assumed static. Sites were surveyed again after a few weeks, and these “monthly” survey events form the primary periods between which occupancy state changes. In years 1 and 2, there were four primary events spanning February to June, and in year 3 there were five primary events during these months. The target species is migratory and enters the river each year and, we hypothesize, increases the proportion of occupied sites as more individuals immigrate and move further upriver.

 We think that two different size groups (small and large) have different initial occupancy and colonization rates. The states are unoccupied (0), occupied by small and large fish (1), and conditional on occupied, occupied only by large fish (2). These states have nothing to do with reproduction, small fish being present is not a result of spawning but due to differential migratory behavior.

 Environmental conditions varied across years, which could lead to initial occupancy for states 1 and 2 to vary across years (or not). Similarly, colonization rates may vary across years as well as by state.

Initially, I ran separate dynamic occupancy models for each size class and each year using colext function from unmarked. However, a reviewer was not satisfied with this approach and suggested that I do not separate the dataset to dataset. Hence, the multistate framework to account for different size groups. But, I am unsure how to set this up so that I can test if initial occupancy or colonization probabilities vary across years. Any suggestions are welcome, as are recommended readings. I have not been able to find an analogous example since most studies only look at primary periods within a single year or treat years as the primary periods.

Thanks in advance.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm working on a multi-season model focusing on a single
species with two years of detection data. Two years before a major fire event,
I collected data for one season, with nine sampling periods across 400+ sites. Some of the sites burned, and some sites were unburned. One year after the fire, I gathered data for a second season at the same sites,
using nine sampling periods. I calculated the proportion of burned area around
each sampled site, ranging from 0 to 1, based on a buffer size approximating the species home range. My goal is to estimate occupancy (psi) relative to the proportion
of burned area using a Before-After Control-Impact design.

In my mind, I need four covariates:

* SiteTreat – binary variable indicating burned (1) or not burned (0).

* Year effect – before or after the fire.

* SeasonSiteTreat – binary interaction for post-fire impact
sites.

* 3-way interaction -- SeasonSiteTreat and 'PropBurned' (continuous
value from 0 to 1).

While I have successfully calculated the first covariate, I
am currently facing a challenge in calculating the year effect and SeasonSiteTreat effect. I created a
matrix for the year effect and inputted it into the unmarked dataframe as
follows:

 yearlySiteCovs <-
list(

    year = matrix(c(

      'year1',
'year2',

      'year1',
'year2',

      'year1',
'year2',

      'year1',
'year2'), nrow= R, ncol=T, byrow=TRUE)

  )

   umf <-
unmarkedMultFrame(y = y,

siteCovs = data.frame(SiteTreat = SiteTreat, PropBurned=PropBurned),

yearlySiteCovs =  yearlySiteCovs,

obsCovs = obs.covs,

                            numPrimary = T)

  year.psi <- colext(psiformula= ~ year, gammaformula = ~ 1, epsilonformula = ~ 1, pformula = ~ 1, data = umf)

However, my attempts to run a model solely with the year
effect on psi have encountered an error message indicating that the object
is not recognized as a matrix, which I identify as 'year' in the model. Specifically, the error states: "Error in model.frame.default(psiformula, siteCovs, na.action = NULL) : object is not a
matrix." I would greatly appreciate any suggestions on creating the year
effect or the SeasonSiteTreat effect in the context of this study.

Many thanks!

Josh

Dear Annika,

I don't think there is a problem, but perhaps modeling the detection component is challenging. Detection is the link between what you observe and what you infer is out there and thus is a critical component of such models.

Your output below suggests that detection probability is very close to zero at the intercept (plogis(-7.4)), and since the scaled year covariate has a strongly positive effect, p will be even smaller for year 1. Therefore, it seems that even without any detection in the first year, the estimates produced are such that high occupancy is a quite likely event.

Overall, I wonder whether this species may not simply be too rare for modeling, with just 0-4 observed detections in ~50 surveyed sites in any given year. In such a multi-species setting, a community occupancy model may be better, though you'd have to fit that with some Bayesian engine like JAGS.

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Re: Estimating psi with a 'year' and 'after-impact' effect in colext?
messages.subject_clean: Estimating psi with a 'year' and 'after-impact' effect in colext?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Josh,

The psiformula is the initial occupancy parameter (what influences occupancy in Year 1)  so it takes SiteCovs instead of YearlySiteCovs. The gammaformula and epsilonformula is where you input the YearlySiteCovs.

I could be wrong but my understanding of the multi-season model is that it is data hungry model and while you have adequate number of sites with only 2 seasons it may be difficult to model what you want to. My suggestion would be to "stack" your data and use a single season model for your analysis. In that framework you could construct a set of models to test if the fire had an impact on psi or if psi changed based on year regardless of fire status.

-Ryan

One year after the fire, I gathered data for a second season at the same sites, using nine sampling periods. I calculated the proportion of burned area around each sampled site, ranging from 0 to 1, based on a buffer size approximating the species home range. >
> * SiteTreat – binary variable indicating burned (1) or not burned (0).
>
> * Year effect – before or after the fire.
>
> * SeasonSiteTreat – binary interaction for post-fire impact sites.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Satavisha,

I am not sure I understand your question. Basically, you can interpret this occupancy model exactly like two logistic regressions. You have one logistic regression for occupancy probability and the other for detection probability.

In a logistic regression, you model a probability as a function of covariates not directly (this would be called with an "identity" link function), but instead with a logit link function. That is, your model looks like this:

logit(p_i) = log(p_i / (1 - p_i) ) = alpha + beta * cov_i + ....,

where p_i and cov_i are the probability and the covariate value, respectively, at site i.

So, yes, to understand how variation in a covariate is associated with variation in the probability, you usually want to use the inverse-link transformation. You can look this up in any book or treatment of logistic regression.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Re: Colonization and extinction having the same behaviour - colext
messages.body_plain:
Colonization is the probability (or rate) of previously unoccupied sites becoming occupied, whereas extinction is the probability (or rate) of previously occupied sites becoming unoccupied. So, no neither is averaging across all sites. Mean colonization is averaged across previously unoccupied sites and mean extinction is averaged across previously occupied sites. If in the initial year occupancy is 0.5 and you have 100 sites in your sample, colonization will be the rate at which the 50 sites that were not occupied became occupied, and extinction is the rate at which the other 50 sites that were occupied became unoccupied.

Hi everyone,

I'm really hoping somebody can please help as I'm quite new to occupancy modelling and unmarked. I have camera trapping data for 29 sites over 4 months and have been running single species models quite easily. However, for one species when using predict to get predicted means and 95% CIs I get huge confidence intervals essentially from 0 to 1 and the predicted mean occupancy is 1. I have 378 detections of this species, which grouped into weekly visits results in 125 presences vs 133 absences. The naive occupancy is 0.86 and the null model occupancy estimate is 0.90, so they're pretty much all over my study area. Plotting the predicted outputs looks like this:

I think this is a boundary estimate issue due to all my sites at the low habitat type being occupied so the estimate is 1. I looked into using penalized likelihood methods but I'm not sure I quite understand how to implement them.

I first tried the MPLE method but when I try to run the computeMPLElambda function I get the following error:

Error in if (any(y < 0 | y > 1)) stop("y values must be 0 <= y <= 1") :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

Is this because I have NAs in the data where cameras were not functioning? If so, is there a way around this?

As this wasn't working for me I also tried the occuPEN_CV method with Ridge and Bayes. I seem to be able to run these but I don't know how to interpret the outputs or get confidence intervals. Following the package documentation, I set up my model as such:

> testCV <- occuPEN_CV(~1 ~LGDpres, deer.data,
                       pen.type="Ridge", foldAssignments=rep(1:5,ceiling(nSites/5))[1:nSites])

Then, running 'testCV @estimates' I get NAs for everything bar the estimate:

Occupancy:
            Estimate SE  z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)    0.748 NA NA      NA
LGDpreslow     8.960 NA NA      NA

I have a feeling this is normal, so continued on to run:

> testCV <- nonparboot(testCV,B=100)
> vcov(testCV,method="nonparboot")

And get the following:

I honestly have no idea if I've done this correctly, if it's useful, how to interpret the output, or how to get the back transformed occupancy estimates and confidence intervals.

If anybody can help me at all, even just pointing me in the right direction I would be extremely grateful. I'm not even sure the penalized methods are the correct option here, but I wasn't sure what else to try first.

Thanks in advance!
Beth

Hey all!

I am also working with an 'unmarkedFramGPC' dataframe and am using 'gpcount' to fit my models. I understand that the predict() function used on the top model outputs M(i) for each site. I am just following up on this chain to ask three quick questions:
I'm looking at the likelihood of the Chandler et al. (2011) model and because availability varies over time, I must have different estimates of available abundance for each primary period that are informing M(i), right? Is the site-specific M(i) an average of the N(i,t)'s?

In AHM volume 1 (Kery and Royle 2016), it is noted that the Chandler et al. (2011) model had been extended to fit binomial mixture models for repeated counts, and the R help file for '?gpcount' specifies that the function "fits the model of Chandler et al. (2011) to repeated count data collected using the robust design." Am I correct in assuming the robust design is the two-tiered design that assumes population closure within primary periods and an open population between prim. periods?

I'm curious if there have been any changes/extensions have been made to extract posteriors for the primary periods to retrieve N(i,t) since this thread was opened?
I want to ensure I understand the conceptual foundation of where my estimates are coming from, and get a gauge on how/if I can estimate the N(i,t) values. I know people aren't often interested in the primary-period abundance estimates, but it is relevant to my study system (as we believe there are seasonal fluctuations), and I am interested in comparing N-mixture prim. pd. estimates to my CMR prim. pd. estimates.

Respectfully,
Megan Novak

On Thursday, December 5, 2013 at 10:01:01 AM UTC-5 Dan Linden wrote:
> I'm not sure if you can extract posteriors for the primary periods from a gpcount model, but generally you are not interested in estimates for the primary periods because you are assuming that the abundance at a site does not change across primary & secondary periods.  The reason there is variation in your observed counts is due to differences in availability and detectability.  The ecological process of interest is abundance, which can only be site specific in a gpcount model.  You need to use pcountOpen if you want period-specific estimates of abundance.

For future reference, the issue was that the model formula included a term like  + I(scale(x)^2) in which scale() was nested inside I(). This works fine for fitting the model but it will not work properly with predict(). I need to look into this more but I believe it is a limitation of R's model.matrix function and not unmarked specifically.

A few possible workarounds:
(1) scale or calculate the squared term manually (or possibly do both) before making your unmarked frame.
(2) Swap the order of scaling and squaring - i.e., square first, then scale.  In the formula:  scale(I(x^2)). This will result in different coefficient estimates, but in my experience, it will usually capture the same pattern in the data.
(3) If you don't need to use predict, or are OK to do the prediction calculations manually, you can use the original formula structure, as the model fitting itself works fine.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lwin,

about your Q1: I may misunderstand you, but I am not sure that using these "IEs" (which I think are just a widespread convention made in camera-trappology) is advisable in an Nmix model. In this model you assume that you can only make one of the two possible measurement errors  -- you can overlook an individual that is there and thus obtain a count that is lower than the true N of the number of individuals in the detection radius of the camtrap during the time period that you call an occasion. But you must never count the same individual twice within the same occasion: that would be a false positive, and that is not allowed by the Nmix model.

Perhaps if you filter/summarize/aggregate your camtrap very aggressively, you can obtain count data that have almost certainly no multiple counts of the same individual within the same occasion ?

Best regards  --- Marc
